subject: Sandbox onramp connectivity advisory — VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN
messages:
From: Lara Nguyen <lara@greenfield.io>
To: marcus_lin@redwood.ai
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-21T16:12:00Z
Subject: Onramp options for our sandbox (low-latency + compliance)

Hi Marcus —

Thanks for taking a look. We spun up a short pilot of Redwood Private in a sandbox account and we need guidance on which connectivity pattern to standardize on across teams. High-level constraints:

- Multi-account AWS (dev/stage/prod) behind Transit Gateway.
- Latency SLO: 20–25 ms p95 for inference requests from our app tier (same region).
- Security: no transitive peering allowed by security policy; anything that creates broad routing visibility needs a strong justification.
- Ops wants an easily testable failover path for maintenance windows.

Attached is a basic network diagram (greenfield-diagram-v1.pdf).

Can you summarize tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN for our setup, and recommend a default pattern for the sandbox that can later be promoted to prod? We care a lot about operational simplicity and predictable egress cost.

Appreciate a short rundown + a checklist we can hand to our infra team.

—Lara
Lara Nguyen
NetOps Lead, Greenfield Analytics

From: marcus_lin@redwood.ai
To: Lara Nguyen <lara@greenfield.io>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-21T17:05:00Z
Subject: Re: Onramp options for our sandbox (low-latency + compliance)

Lara — thanks for the clear constraints and the diagram. Quick executive summary first, then details and a proposed runbook: see attached (redwood-conn-options-summary.pdf).

Executive recommendation (sandbox -> canonical pattern to promote):
- Control plane and management traffic: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) from customer VPCs into a dedicated Redwood endpoint VPC (restrict by security groups).
- Data plane (latency-sensitive inference traffic within same region/account): VPC Peering between the customer workload VPC and a dedicated inference VPC (if both are in the same AWS account/region).
- Cross-account / cross-region: fall back to PrivateLink or dedicated inter-region peering + regional inference pools.
- On-prem / remote sites: Site-to-site VPN as a soft-failover (works, but higher latency and more variability).

Why this hybrid approach?
- PrivateLink gives strong isolation and explicit endpoint controls (fits your "no transitive peering" policy). It also avoids exposing subnets via route tables and is compatible with cross-account setups without opening broad routing.
- VPC Peering is lowest-latency inside the same region/account and has minimal packet overhead — good for meeting the 20–25 ms p95 when the workload and inference nodes are nearby. But peering does create routing relationships that need governance (that's why I recommend limiting peering to specific workload–inference pairs, not hub-style peering).
- S2S VPN is reliable for on-prem and DR, but: variable latency, NAT + throughput limits, and more operational baggage. Best used as fallback or for environments that can't use PrivateLink.

Key operational notes and tradeoffs:
- Egress/costs: PrivateLink charges per-hour + per-GB. VPC Peering is typically cheaper for high-volume token traffic (no per-endpoint GB charge). Evaluate expected token volume to decide default.
- Security posture: PrivateLink aligns with "no transitive peering"; provide explicit SGs and endpoint policies. Peering requires strict route/ACL governance to avoid inadvertent transit.
- Observability: Peering traffic will show up as VPC flow logs; PrivateLink traffic appears as endpoint flow and requires endpoint-level logging hooks.
- Failover: PrivateLink + peering combine well — peering for performance, PrivateLink as control-plane anchor and cross-account path.

Proposed sandbox checklist (high-level):
1) Create Redwood endpoint VPC (single account) — allocate interface endpoints for control-plane APIs.
2) For each sandbox workload VPC in the same region/account: create a VPC peering to the dedicated inference VPC, add minimal routes, and restrict with SGs.
3) For cross-account sandboxes or teams behind Transit GW that disallow peering: create PrivateLink endpoints (customer side) to the Redwood endpoint VPC.
4) Configure S2S VPN only for on-prem sites or as a documented fallback path.
5) Validate latency with a small synthetic test (10k requests across p95 window) and compare peering vs PrivateLink.
6) Document cost estimation for expected token volumes and make a choice before promoting to prod.

A couple of questions for you that will help us finalize:
- Are your sandbox workloads in the same AWS account as the sandbox inference VPC, or are they split across accounts behind Transit Gateway?
- Do you prefer a single "inference VPC" in our account, or separate inference VPCs per environment (dev/stage/prod)?

I copied Kim (kimberly_park) for the onramp operational checklist and Neha (neha_kapoor) for security sign-off once we lock a pattern. I'll follow up with a one-page runbook and expected cost examples.

—Marcus Lin
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
redwood.ai
Attachment: redwood-conn-options-summary.pdf

From: Lara Nguyen <lara@greenfield.io>
To: marcus_lin@redwood.ai
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, Tom Alvarez <tom.alvarez@greenfield.io>
Date: 2027-06-21T18:02:00Z
Subject: Re: Onramp options for our sandbox (low-latency + compliance)

Thanks Marcus — this is very helpful. A couple clarifications from our side:

- Our sandbox workload VPCs are currently split across two AWS accounts (dev + staging) but in the same region. The transit team currently uses TGW and has policies that forbid peering across accounts (they want centralized routing via TGW).
- Security has a hard constraint: no broad route propagation. Theyve said interface endpoints are acceptable because they provide narrow scoping.
- For latency testing: we can spin up a small inference pool in the staging account if needed; ops prefers not to open peering for sandbox yet.

Can you produce a short ops checklist we can hand to TGW owners and the infra team that shows steps for PrivateLink-only onramp (what needs to be done in the TGW account vs the workload accounts vs Redwood side)? Also curious if PrivateLink will add latency that breaches our 20–25 ms p95 target. If you have a quick synthetic test plan we can run in staging, that would be ideal.

—Lara

From: marcus_lin@redwood.ai
To: Lara Nguyen <lara@greenfield.io>
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.ai, neha_kapoor@redwood.ai
Date: 2027-06-21T20:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Onramp options for our sandbox (low-latency + compliance)

Lara — good constraints, thanks. Given TGW rules and the security team's preference, PrivateLink-first is the practical path for sandbox promotion. Below is a concise TGW-friendly ops checklist and a lightweight synthetic test plan you can run in staging. Ill also attach a one-page runbook (runbook-onramp-checklist.md).

PrivateLink-first ops checklist (TGW / multi-account):
- TGW owners:
  - Ensure the TGW attachment for the workload account does NOT propagate routes to the Redwood endpoint VPC (avoid transitive routing).
  - If you want centralized endpoints, create a dedicated endpoint VPC in the TGW account and host the interface endpoints there; attach that VPC to TGW and control propagation.
- Workload account owners (dev/stage):
  - Create VPC interface endpoints that point to the Redwood endpoint services (we will provide service names and endpoint policy templates).
  - Configure endpoint security groups to only allow inference traffic from the workload subnets.
- Redwood side (our infra):
  - Provide service names and a whitelist of allowed principals (account IDs).
  - Configure endpoint acceptance and endpoint-level logging (we can push logs to your central S3 if you prefer).

Latency test (staging synthetic):
1) Deploy a small inference pool in staging (2–4 instances) colocated with the workload subnets.
2) From a test client in the workload VPC, run a 5k request workload that approximates your typical prompt size (measure p50/p95/p99).
3) Repeat the test with: (a) PrivateLink interface endpoint, (b) same setup but with a temporary peering in a throwaway account (if security allows) to compare delta.
4) Capture CPU/GPU utilization, round-trip latency, and egress bytes.

Expected outcome: PrivateLink typically adds ~1–6 ms of overhead vs direct peering depending on path and security group processing. For well-provisioned regional inference pools you should remain within 20–25 ms p95, but the synthetic run will give us the definitive number.

Next steps:
- Ill prepare a short one-page TGW-oriented checklist + endpoint policy templates by EOD tomorrow.
- Kim: can you confirm whether we need a dedicated endpoint VPC in the TGW account or if tenant teams will create endpoints directly in their accounts?
- Neha: after we finalize the checklist, wed like a quick security review sign-off.

—Marcus
Sr. Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
Attachment: runbook-onramp-checklist.md
